cards.explanation: The question is whether it's better to have seventy men rule, all of Jerubbaal's sons, or just one man. Abimelech, son of Jerubbaal, wants his uncles to put that to the leaders of Shechem. Then he adds, “Remember that I am your own flesh and blood.” I think he's tilting the question toward himself before anybody answers. Friends, that's a pitch with the answer already baked in.

The reason is that he's their brother. The text says the leaders of Shechem were inclined to follow Abimelech because “He is our brother.” That's the reason they give, not his record and not his wisdom. I think a family tie can feel like plenty when someone's selling it hard.

The answer is Baal-berith. The seventy shekels of silver come from the temple of Baal-berith, a false god. The silver for this plan comes straight out of a temple, and I think that tells you where Shechem's heart is sitting. Hold on to that detail, friends.

The answer is True. Abimelech hired some “…worthless and reckless men to follow him.” That's what the seventy shekels buy: a crew. I think when a man has to pay for his followers, that tells you something about his leadership.
The answer is that he hid himself. Jotham, the youngest son of Jerubbaal, survived because he hid himself. The text gives that reason and no other. I think he had a lot to carry after it.

The answer is king. The leaders of Shechem and Beth-millo gathered beside the oak at the pillar and proceeded to make Abimelech their king. That's the word the text uses. It's a big title for a man whose crew was hired with silver from a temple.

The answer is the top of Mount Gerizim. Jotham climbs up there, raises his voice and cries out. His first words are, “Listen to me, O leaders of Shechem, and may God listen to you.” I think a man who hid while his brothers were murdered has decided he's done staying quiet.

The olive tree won't stop giving its oil to rule. It says, “Should I stop giving my oil that honors both God and man, to hold sway over the trees?” Its answer is a question, and it's a no in disguise. I think it'd rather keep making oil than rule.

The answer is False. In Jotham's story, the fig tree asks, “Should I stop giving my sweetness and my good fruit, to hold sway over the trees?” It keeps its sweetness and its good fruit and doesn't take the job. Nobody's lining up for this one.

The answer is wine. The grapevine says, “Should I stop giving my wine that cheers both God and man, to hold sway over the trees?” Same pattern as the olive and the fig. The grapevine has its work, and it keeps it.

The thornbush tells the trees to find refuge in its shade. It says, “…come and find refuge in my shade.” That's the offer, with an if attached. Friends, I've got a lot of questions about how much shade a thornbush can really give. But that's the offer in the story.
The answer is stone. Jotham says the seventy sons were killed on a single stone. I think this one hurts, and it's a heavy part of the story. It's a hard line to hear.

The answer is True. Jotham says they made Abimelech, “…the son of his maidservant…” king “…because he is your brother…” That's the same reason the leaders gave back in verse 3. Jotham is holding it up to the light.

Jotham says they may rejoice in Abimelech, and he in them. His words are, “…then may you rejoice in Abimelech, and he in you.” That's the good side of his if. It only holds if they've acted faithfully and honestly toward Jerubbaal and his house. The condition is the whole point.

The answer is fire. Jotham says, “…may fire come from Abimelech and consume the leaders of Shechem and Beth-millo…” and may fire come from the leaders and consume Abimelech. It goes both ways. Fire also showed up in the thornbush's words, so Jotham's story and his message are tied together.

The answer is Beer. After his message from Mount Gerizim, Jotham ran away, escaping to Beer, and he lived there. That's where this passage leaves him. I think after speaking up like that, he didn't hang around for the replies.

He stays in Beer out of fear of his brother Abimelech. The text says Jotham “…lived there for fear of his brother Abimelech.” Abimelech is the brother who murdered his seventy brothers, so I think that fear makes sense. Fear is the reason the text gives for his staying in Beer.
